doc.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
title: Name bands and Louis Armstrong's pass
summary: The kids' show gives him a view of the big bands, encouragement from their players and a pass from Armstrong, though he idolised cornetist Del Staigers.

bands.name: Erskine Hawkins and the Bama State Collegians

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: That’s not in your bio, you know. It doesn’t say, “played with Duke Ellington.”
There are many things I just never even thought to mention, but it’s fantastic.
I was going to say, that’s interesting. At the age of whatever it was, 13, you were playing with Duke Ellington.

Yeah. In a sense, yeah. And they were always – they were very encouraging. All those fellows – Count Basie’s band, Erskine Hawkins and the Bama State Collegians – they would all – they would say, “Kid, you stick with it.” And they remembered me when I finally became a professional player. They’d say, “I remember you from that children’s program.” And Louis, he remembered me. He’d say, “I remember you when you was a little boy.” He was great. He came to – I came to Witham Theater, and they introduced me to him. So he gave me a pass. He said, “You come and see Pops every day. Just show them this pass, and they’ll let you in.” At that time, I was interested – I wanted to play like Del Staigers, who was a cornet soloist. I was really impressed with that. I just didn’t know what jazz was, basically, and I didn’t know classical either, but I knew that I happened to like Del Staigers. So I wanted to play The Carnival of Venice and things like that. I only went to see Louis that one time, with the pass. I heard him, and I was impressed, but it never occurred to me to try to play like him at that time. Many years later, I began to realize what a great person he was. It’s funny.
But you had a different idea of what music was at that age. About how old were you when you were doing all of this, when you were playing on the kids’ show?

I think I played on there until I was about 15. Then it wasn’t too long after that that I think they discontinued it. But it went for many years. It was at least a source for the young kids to get a chance to develop their talents.
Did you get paid for it? Or was it – no, it was just more or less a talent show.
No, we didn’t get paid for it. As a matter of fact, it was just more or less an advertisement for the tailoring company, for Parisian Tailors, and it made them quite popular, too.
